what’s going on? phrase

also what’s going on here?, what’s happening?, what’s up?, what’s the matter?, what’s all this?, know the score, he doesn’t know what the score is, what’s happening, know what’s going on

classical

Plaut. Most. 2.2.27; Plaut. Capt. 3.5.11: quid negōtī est, quamobrem suscēnsēs mihi? (Lewis & Short), s.v. negōtium
Traupman 99
Traupman 322

Quid negōtī est?

negōtī, partitive genitive of negōtium (the older form of negōtiī)

what’s the matter? what’s going on?

Other words

  • quid agātur — what is going on, what is being done

    indirect question with the passive of agō, after scīre, vidēre, nescīre · classical · Cic. Mur. 83: est tuum, Catō, vidēre quid agātur (Lewis & Short s.v. sum); Cic. Att. 3.8.2: nunc istīc quid agātur, magnopere timeō (Lewis & Short s.v. timeō); Traupman 107: he doesn’t know what the score is, nescit quid agātur

    “What is being done”: the impersonal passive of agō covers what English calls “what’s happening”. As a direct question, quid agitur?.

  • Quid agitur? — what’s going on? how are things?

    also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 373–374: Hem, Dēmea, haud aspexeram tē. Quid agitur?; Traupman 99; Traupman 322

    In comedy also the greeting “how are things?” (see how are you).

  • Quid reī (hīc) est? — what’s going on here?

    reī, partitive genitive of rēs · also used · classical · Plaut. Epid. 203; Plaut. Merc. 964: Quid reī est?; Liv. 3.48.4: quid hoc reī sit (Lewis & Short s.v. percontor); Traupman 99; Traupman 191: Quid reī est?; Traupman 322

    Plautus’s question, without hīc; with hoc, “what is all this?”.

Examples

  • Hem, Dēmea, haud aspexeram tē. Quid agitur?

    Oh, Demea, I didn’t see you. How are things?Ter. Ad. 373–374

  • Quid ibi fīēbat?

    What was going on there?Traupman 190

See also what happened?, how are you?, oh!.
